qa.question:
At the northern extension zone of the Chaah Mine, the group is commencing with 
underground mining while also transitioning the Southern Pit from open-pit to underground 
mining. The group has appointed a turnkey contractor to undertake full mining operations.  
 
(i) 
Under the turnkey contractor model, how are operational responsibilities 
and performance accountability allocated between the contractor and the 
group? In particular, who controls mine planning, production scheduling 
and execution, and what performance measures or contractual obligations 
are used to ensure that the contractor delivers the targeted production 
levels? How are cost overruns, production shortfalls and operational risks 
allocated between the contractor and the group, and what protections does 
the group have against cost escalation or underperformance? 
 
(ii) 
With the transition to underground mining, what are management's 
projected C1 cash cost and all-in cash cost per tonne? 
 
In his message to shareholders, the managing director noted that underground ore 
extraction continued during the year, with approximately 48,700 tonnes extracted in the 
fourth quarter. 
 
(iii) 
Can management provide greater clarity on the total production from the 
Chaah, Kahang and Gerik mines in FY2026?
qa.answer:
At the northern extension zone of the Chaah Mine, the group is commencing with underground 
mining while also transitioning the Southern Pit from open-pit to underground mining. The 
group has appointed a turnkey contractor to undertake full mining operations. 
 
(i) 
Under the turnkey contractor model, how are operational responsibilities and 
performance accountability allocated between the contractor and the group? In 
particular, who controls mine planning, production scheduling and execution, and what 
performance measures or contractual obligations are used to ensure that the contractor 
delivers the targeted production levels? How are cost overruns, production shortfalls 
and operational risks allocated between the contractor and the group, and what 
protections does the group have against cost escalation or underperformance? 
 
The Group has adopted a comprehensive turnkey contractor arrangement for its underground 
mining operations at the Chaah Mine, encompassing underground mine design, determination 
of mining methods, production scheduling, mining sequencing and execution, ore extraction, 
hauling, crushing, screening and processing, as well as the upgrading of the existing processing 
plant. 
 
Under this arrangement, the contractor is responsible for developing the underground mine 
design and determining the appropriate mining methods, which are required to be endorsed by 
a qualified engineer appointed by the contractor and subsequently approved by the Group. The 
contractor is also responsible for production scheduling, mining sequencing and the day-to-day 
execution of mining and processing operations. 
 
In addition, the contractor is fully responsible for developing the underground mining 
infrastructure necessary to support its operations, including mine access roads, water 
management ponds, ventilation systems and other associated infrastructure. 
 
The Group retains overall oversight of the mine, including the review and approval of mine 
designs and mining methods, monitoring of operational performance, safety oversight and the 
sale of iron ore products. 
 
The contractor is responsible for funding the development of the underground mining 
infrastructure and the upgrading of the existing processing plant, with no funding contribution 
required from the Group under the agreed arrangement. The Group may, where appropriate, 
facilitate the procurement of certain materials on behalf of the contractor. Any financial 
assistance from the Group, if considered necessary, would be at the Group's discretion and 
subject to the applicable approval procedures. 

 
 
 
The contractor's payout is linked to the sale of iron ore products rather than solely to the volume 
of ore extracted or processed. This arrangement is intended to align the contractor's commercial 
interests with the Group's sales performance and reduce the Group's exposure to fixed 
operating costs. 
 
Under the turnkey arrangement, the contractor assumes responsibility for operational risks 
associated with the contracted mining and processing activities. The contract does not provide 
for additional payments arising solely from cost overruns or cost escalation incurred by the 
contractor. 
 
The contractor is also subject to contractual penalties should production fall short of the agreed 
targets within specified timeframes. These provisions are intended to promote performance 
accountability and provide the Group with contractual protection against production 
underperformance. 
 
The Group continues to monitor the contractor's performance against the agreed production 
targets, operational requirements and applicable safety and technical standards to support the 
achievement of its production objectives. 
 
(ii) 
With the transition to underground mining, what are management's projected C1 cash 
cost and all-in cash cost per tonne? 
 
It is not currently the Group's practice to provide forward-looking projections of operating cash 
costs or all-in cash costs per tonne. Furthermore, as certain terms of the turnkey contractor 
arrangement are commercially sensitive, the Group does not consider it appropriate to disclose 
such projections. 
 
The Group is progressing with its transition to commercial underground mining operations at 
the Chaah Mine, which is currently expected to commence in the third quarter of FY2027. The 
commencement timeline, previously targeted for the second quarter of FY2027, has been 
revised to the third quarter of FY2027 due to delays in the upgrading of the conveyor belt system.  
 
As the conveyor belt upgrading works and development of underground mining infrastructure 
and processing plant remain in progress, the Group has yet to establish a sufficiently 
representative operating baseline from which reliable unit cost projections can be derived. 
 
Management will continue to monitor production performance, operating expenditure and cost 
efficiency as underground mining operations progress. Subject to the availability of meaningful 
operating data, the Group intends to provide an appropriate analysis of its operating 
performance and cost structure in the Management Discussion and Analysis accompanying its 
1H FY2027 financial results announcement. 
 
In his message to shareholders, the managing director noted that underground ore extraction 
continued during the year, with approximately 48,700 tonnes extracted in the fourth quarter. 
 
(iii) 
Can management provide greater clarity on the total production from the Chaah, Kahang 
and Gerik mines in FY2026? 
 
During FY2026, the Group's mining activities and production performance across its operating 
sites were as follows: 
 
Chaah Mine (Iron Ore) 
During FY2026, approximately 371,200 tonnes of ore were extracted in the course of the 
ongoing underground mine development works, including approximately 48,700 tonnes in the 
fourth quarter. These quantities represent ore extracted during development activities rather 
than full-scale commercial underground mining operations. A portion of the extracted ore was 
processed into approximately 141,900 tonnes of iron ore concentrate during the financial year. 
 
Kahang Mine (Bauxite) 
No new bauxite production was recorded during FY2026. However, the Group sold 
approximately 53,300 dry metric tonnes of bauxite from stockpile inventory carried forward from 
FY2025. 

 
 
 
Gerik Mine (Rare Earths) 
MCRE Resources Sdn. Bhd., in which the Group holds a 40% interest, produced approximately 
11,900 wet tonnes of rare earth carbonate from Parcels 1 and 2 during FY2026. This represents 
MCRE's total production rather than the Group's 40% attributable share. 
 
The Group wishes to highlight that ore extraction, processed product output and sales volumes 
represent different operating measures and should not be directly aggregated when assessing 
production performance across the respective mines

of MCRE's revenue, expenses, assets and liabilities.  
 
(i) 
As a joint operation, what is the group's actual involvement in MCRE's 
operations 
and

decision-making? 
Specifically, 
what

During the year, MCRE produced approximately 3,600 wet tonnes of rare earth carbonate 
from Parcels 1 and 2. Development work has commenced at Parcel 3, with operations 
targeted to commence by the middle of FY2027. However, MCRE’s export permit expired in 
June 2026. 
 
(ii) 
Who was responsible for securing the renewal of MCRE's export permit, and 
why was the renewal not obtained before its expiry?  
 
(iii)

affected its ability to sell and export rare earth carbonate, and what is its 
current working capital position? Does MCRE have sufficient financial

At the Gerik Mine in Hulu Perak, MCRE’s operations were subject to temporary work 
suspension orders. Operations resumed in January 2026 after MCRE addressed the matters

(iv) 
Following the regulatory suspension, how has the board independently 
assessed whether MCRE's environmental and operational controls are

independent 
technical 
expertise, 
site 
inspections 
and 
assurance

qa.answer:
Following completion of the acquisition on 12 September 2025, MCRE Resources Sdn. Bhd. 
(“MCRE”) is accounted for as a joint operation, with the group recognising its 40% share of 
MCRE's revenue, expenses, assets and liabilities. 
 
(i) 
As a joint operation, what is the group's actual involvement in MCRE's operations and 
strategic decision-making? Specifically, what responsibilities does the group assume in 
operational management, technical oversight, financing and capital commitments? 
 
Following completion of the acquisition on 12 September 2025, the Group holds a 40% equity 
interest in MCRE. Having regard to the Group's ownership interest and the rights and 
obligations established under the Shareholders' Agreement entered into with the other 
shareholders, MCRE is accounted for as a joint operation in accordance with the applicable 
accounting standards. 
 
MCRE's day-to-day mining operations, including the implementation of the specialised in-situ 
leaching methodology and related technical processes, are managed by MCRE's own 
management and technical teams, with technical support from its technical partner in China. 
 
Given the specialised nature of these mining processes, the Group's appointed representatives 
on MCRE's Board of Directors do not directly undertake technical supervision or day-to-day 
operational management. Nevertheless, they participate in MCRE's corporate governance and 
monitor its overall operational and financial performance, development progress and relevant 
regulatory matters. 
 
In relation to strategic decision-making, under the Shareholders' Agreement, certain strategic 
and material decisions concerning MCRE require the Group's approval, having regard to its 40% 
shareholding. 
 
With respect to financing and capital commitments, the Group's responsibilities are determined 
by the relevant provisions of the Shareholders' Agreement and other applicable contractual 
arrangements. Any additional funding requirements would be assessed in accordance with 
these arrangements, the Group's financial position and applicable approval procedures. 
 
The Group continues to exercise its rights and responsibilities under the joint operation 
arrangements while maintaining oversight of MCRE's overall performance through the 
established governance framework. 
 
During the year, MCRE produced approximately 3,600 wet tonnes of rare earth carbonate from 
Parcels 1 and 2. Development work has commenced at Parcel 3, with operations targeted to 
commence by the middle of FY2027. However, MCRE’s export permit expired in June 2026. 
 
(ii) 
Who was responsible for securing the renewal of MCRE's export permit, and why was 
the renewal not obtained before its expiry? 
 
The applications for export permits are undertaken by MCRE's management team, which is 
responsible for their preparation, submission and follow-up with the relevant Malaysian 
authorities. 
 
MCRE submitted separate applications for new export permits in December 2025 and May 
2026, prior to the expiry of its existing export permit in June 2026. MCRE also sought an 
extension of the existing permit. Notwithstanding these applications and the various 

 
 
engagements undertaken by MCRE's management with the relevant authorities, the necessary 
approvals were not obtained before the expiry of the existing permit. 
 
Following the introduction of new export permit guidelines by the Ministry of Natural Resources 
and Environmental Sustainability of Malaysia (“NRES”), effective 1 October 2026, MCRE has 
continued to engage the relevant authorities regarding the applicable regulatory requirements 
and the status of its outstanding applications. 
 
In parallel, MCRE is undertaking preparatory work to evaluate the possibility of pursuing judicial 
review in relation to the export permit matter. The respective Boards of Directors of MCRE and 
the Group have agreed to proceed with such preparatory work. However, no decision has been 
made to commence judicial review proceedings at this stage. 
 
As the issuance of export permits is subject to the approval of the relevant authorities, there 
can be no assurance as to the timing or outcome of MCRE's applications. 
 
(iii) 
With MCRE's export permit having expired in June 2026, how has this affected its ability 
to sell and export rare earth carbonate, and what is its current working capital position? 
Does MCRE have sufficient financial resources to sustain its existing operations and 
complete the development of Parcel 3 without further funding from the joint operators? 
 
Following the expiry of MCRE's existing export permit in June 2026, MCRE has been unable to 
resume exports of its rare earth carbonate products to China pending approval of the relevant 
export permit applications. Consequently, its ability to generate revenue and cash inflows from 
these exports has been affected. 
 
Notwithstanding the export restrictions, mining and production activities at the Gerik Mine have 
continued, although at a reduced scale. However, the prolonged delay in obtaining the 
necessary export approvals has placed increasing pressure on MCRE's working capital position. 
 
Based on the latest cash flow projections provided by MCRE's management, while MCRE 
continues to fund its current operations, its ability to sustain these activities over the coming 
months will depend on its available financial resources and the outcome of measures being 
pursued to address its working capital requirements. 
 
MCRE's management is actively evaluating various options, including potential financing and 
other commercial arrangements, to address its working capital requirements and support 
operational continuity. 
 
In view of the prevailing circumstances, MCRE has recently deferred further development 
activities at Parcel 3 pending greater clarity on its financial resources and the matter relating to 
the export permit. The timing for resumption of these activities will be assessed by MCRE's 
management as circumstances develop. 
 
Accordingly, MCRE is not presently in a position to confirm that its existing operations and the 
planned development of Parcel 3 can be sustained or completed without additional funding. 
The Group's Board continues to monitor developments and assess the potential implications 
for the Group. 
 
 
At the Gerik Mine in Hulu Perak, MCRE’s operations were subject to temporary work suspension 
orders. Operations resumed in January 2026 after MCRE addressed the matters identified by the 
authorities. 
 
(iv) 
Following the regulatory suspension, how has the board independently assessed 
whether MCRE's environmental and operational controls are adequate to prevent a 
recurrence? Given that the independent directors do not appear to have direct mining or 
resource extraction experience, what independent technical expertise, site inspections 
and assurance mechanisms have they relied upon to discharge their oversight 
responsibilities? 
 

 
 
MCRE is responsible for the management of its mining operations and the implementation of 
environmental and operational controls at the Gerik Mine, including compliance with the 
applicable regulatory requirements and approval conditions. 
 
The Group understands that, pursuant to the applicable environmental approval conditions, 
MCRE is required to undertake periodic environmental compliance audits. These audits are 
conducted by an independent third-party consultant, and the relevant reports are submitted 
directly to the Department of Environment Malaysia (“DOE”), with copies provided to MCRE. 
 
Following the temporary suspension of operations, MCRE addressed the matters identified by 
the relevant authorities, following which operations resumed in January 2026. 
 
Given the specialised nature of MCRE's mining activities, the Group's Board recognises the 
importance of independent technical assessments in supporting its oversight responsibilities. 
In light of the previous regulatory suspension, the Group has requested that copies of the 
relevant environmental compliance audit reports be provided to its Board of Directors for review. 
The Group has also requested access to MCRE's environmental consultants and independent 
auditors, where necessary, to facilitate clarification of material compliance findings, corrective 
measures and any outstanding issues. 
 
These measures are intended to strengthen the Group's access to independent technical 
information and support its ongoing oversight of MCRE through the established governance 
arrangements

qa.question:
The group’s joint ventures include Rigid Temau Sdn. Bhd. (RTSB), Maha Hijau Sdn. Bhd. 
(MH), Southern Atlantic Metal Sdn. Bhd. and Sri Aman Minerals Sdn. Bhd.  
 
On 28 September 2022, the group acquired a 50% interest in RTSB for RM7.16 million in 
cash and settled a further RM4.84 million, representing its 50% share of advances previously 
provided by the vendors to RTSB. RTSB commenced iron ore production in August 2023, but 
its mining licence subsequently expired. In addition to impairing the carrying value of the 
joint venture, the group recognised a RM16.2 million provision against amounts due from 
RTSB. 
 
As at 31 July 2026, the carrying value of the group's investments in joint ventures had been 
fully impaired to nil. All four joint ventures have unrecognised share of loss, amounting to 
an aggregate of RM5.56 million.   
 
(Compiled from company annual reports)  

In addition to the expiry of RTSB’s licence, the exploration licences of Maha Hijau, Southern 
Atlantic Metal and Sri Aman Minerals were not renewed 1, resulting in corresponding 
impairment losses in FY2025.  
 
(i) 
Can management clarify when exactly RTSB's mining licence expired, why it 
was not renewed and what efforts were made by RTSB to secure its renewal 
before expiry? Given the group's 50% interest in RTSB, what oversight did 
management and the board exercise over the joint venture's licence 
renewal process, and why was the risk of losing the licence not addressed in 
time? 
 
The group's investment in RTSB has resulted in a fully impaired joint venture carrying value 
and a RM16.2 million provision against amounts due from RTSB.  
 
(ii) 
What was the original RTSB investment case, including the expected 
production profile, mine life and financial returns, and how did actual 
performance compare with the investment assumptions? Has the board 
reviewed whether the original due diligence and subsequent monitoring 
were adequate, and what lessons have been incorporated into the group's 
investment approval process, especially for joint ventures? 
 
(iii) 
How has the board assessed whether management has the capacity, 
capabilities and execution track record to oversee the critical transition to 
underground mining at the Chaah Mine and acquire a new REE mine while 
also managing the group's joint venture investments? 
 
(iv) 
In light of the significant losses incurred on the group's joint venture 
investments, should the group suspend further joint venture investments 
until it has demonstrated that it has the necessary capabilities and oversight 
arrangements to manage them effectively?

qa.answer:
The group’s joint ventures include Rigid Temau Sdn. Bhd. (“RTSB”), Maha Hijau Sdn. Bhd. 
(“MH”), Southern Atlantic Metal Sdn. Bhd. and Sri Aman Minerals Sdn. Bhd. 
 
On 28 September 2022, the group acquired a 50% interest in RTSB for RM7.16 million in cash 
and settled a further RM4.84 million, representing its 50% share of advances previously provided 
by the vendors to RTSB. RTSB commenced iron ore production in August 2023, but its mining 
licence subsequently expired. In addition to impairing the carrying value of the joint venture, the 
group recognised a RM16.2 million provision against amounts due from RTSB. 
 
As at 31 July 2026, the carrying value of the group's investments in joint ventures had been fully 
impaired to nil. All four joint ventures have unrecognised share of loss, amounting to an 
aggregate of RM5.56 million. 
 
 
(Compiled from company annual reports) 
 
In addition to the expiry of RTSB’s licence, the exploration licences of MH, Southern Atlantic 
Metal and Sri Aman Minerals were not renewed¹, resulting in corresponding impairment losses 
in FY2025. 
 

 
 
(i) 
Can management clarify when exactly RTSB's mining licence expired, why it was not 
renewed and what efforts were made by RTSB to secure its renewal before expiry? Given 
the group's 50% interest in RTSB, what oversight did management and the board 
exercise over the joint venture's licence renewal process, and why was the risk of losing 
the licence not addressed in time? 
 
RTSB undertook its mining operations pursuant to a sub-mining operator arrangement, under 
which the underlying mining leases were held by another party. Accordingly, the renewal of the 
mining leases was subject to the relevant regulatory processes and arrangements involving the 
underlying lease holder and other relevant parties. 
 
The renewal of the affected mining lease was subsequently impacted by changes in the 
administrative arrangements governing mining rights in the State of Pahang, which gave rise to 
a dispute concerning the relevant mining rights. The matter is currently the subject of ongoing 
legal proceedings. 
 
The Group participates in RTSB's governance through its appointed representatives on RTSB's 
Board of Directors, while the day-to-day mining operations and related administrative matters 
are managed by RTSB's management and the relevant operating parties. 
 
The Group was aware of the issues affecting the mining rights and supported RTSB's decision 
to pursue the available legal remedies to protect its interests. 
 
Given that the matter remains before the courts, the Group considers it inappropriate to 
comment further on the specific circumstances of the dispute or the respective positions of the 
parties involved. The Group will continue to monitor material developments and assess their 
implications for its investment in RTSB. 
 
 
The group's investment in RTSB has resulted in a fully impaired joint venture carrying value and 
a RM16.2 million provision against amounts due from RTSB. 
 
(ii) 
What was the original RTSB investment case, including the expected production profile, 
mine life and financial returns, and how did actual performance compare with the 
investment assumptions? Has the board reviewed whether the original due diligence 
and subsequent monitoring were adequate, and what lessons have been incorporated 
into the group's investment approval process, especially for joint ventures? 
The original investment was undertaken with the objective of expanding the Group's iron ore 
mining portfolio through access to several mining areas. In evaluating the investment, the Group 
considered the acquisition consideration, anticipated production potential, expected financial 
returns and prevailing iron ore market conditions, based on the information available at the time. 
 
RTSB subsequently commenced iron ore production in August 2023. However, its operating 
performance fell short of the original expectations, particularly following the developments 
affecting the underlying mining rights and the resulting legal proceedings. 
 
Although the legal proceedings remain ongoing and discussions among the relevant parties 
concerning possible solutions are continuing, uncertainty remains regarding the timing and 
outcome of any resolution. Accordingly, the Group adopted a prudent approach in assessing 
the recoverability of its investment and related advances, resulting in the impairment and 
provision recognised in FY2026. 
 
The RTSB experience has highlighted the importance of evaluating not only the commercial 
potential of mining investments but also the continuity of underlying mining rights, contractual 
arrangements and regulatory risks, particularly where mining rights are held by parties outside 
the joint venture. 
 
The Group will continue to review and, where appropriate, strengthen its investment evaluation 
and post-investment monitoring processes, including the assessment of mining tenure, 

 
 
contractual rights, regulatory developments and the timely escalation of material risks to the 
Board. 
 
(iii) 
How has the board assessed whether management has the capacity, capabilities and 
execution track record to oversee the critical transition to underground mining at the 
Chaah Mine and acquire a new REE mine while also managing the group's joint venture 
investments? 
The Board recognises that the Group's mining and resource activities require appropriate 
technical expertise, operational capabilities and management oversight, particularly given the 
transition to underground mining at the Chaah Mine and the expansion of its rare earth business. 
 
The Group's operating model is structured to draw upon the resources and expertise of 
dedicated operational teams, specialised contractors and technical partners, rather than relying 
solely on the Group's central management team to directly undertake all operational activities. 
 
At the Chaah Mine, the Group has engaged a turnkey mining contractor responsible for the 
planning and execution of underground mining operations, including the relevant mining 
infrastructure and processing activities. This arrangement enables the Group to leverage the 
contractor's specialised technical expertise and operational resources, while the Group retains 
oversight of overall operational performance, safety and compliance matters. 
 
For its rare earth operations, MCRE has its own management and technical arrangements 
responsible for the day-to-day mining activities. The Group participates in the governance and 
monitoring of MCRE through its interests and representation under the applicable joint 
operation arrangements. 
 
Similarly, the Group's other joint venture investments are managed through their respective 
operating and governance arrangements, with the Group's involvement reflecting the nature of 
each investment and the applicable contractual rights and responsibilities. 
 
The Board oversees the Group's overall business strategy, material investment decisions and 
risk management, while management is responsible for coordinating the implementation of 
approved business plans and monitoring the performance of the Group's operations and 
investments. 
 
As the Group's mining and resource activities progress, the Board will continue to assess the 
adequacy of its management resources, technical capabilities and governance arrangements, 
and consider additional specialist support where appropriate. 
 
(iv) 
In light of the significant losses incurred on the group's joint venture investments, 
should the group suspend further joint venture investments until it has demonstrated 
that it has the necessary capabilities and oversight arrangements to manage them 
effectively? 
 
The Group acknowledges the losses recognised in relation to certain joint venture investments 
and recognises the importance of prudent investment evaluation, risk management and 
appropriate governance arrangements. 
 
However, the Board does not consider that a blanket suspension of future joint venture 
investments would necessarily be in the best interests of the Group and its shareholders. Joint 
ventures remain a potential avenue for the Group to pursue viable strategic opportunities, 
particularly where strategic collaboration with suitable partners provides access to mineral 
resources, technical expertise, operational capabilities and other complementary resources. 
 
The Group recognises that the experience gained from its existing joint venture investments 
highlights the importance of carefully assessing not only the commercial potential of an 
investment but also the underlying mining rights, regulatory requirements, contractual 
arrangements and the ability to exercise appropriate oversight. 
 
Accordingly, any future joint venture investment will be evaluated on its individual merits, taking 
into consideration its strategic alignment, commercial viability, financial commitments, 

 
 
regulatory and operational risks, as well as the availability of the necessary technical and 
management resources. 
 
Particular attention will also be given to the proposed governance arrangements, including the 
Group's contractual rights, access to relevant operational and financial information, and 
mechanisms for monitoring material developments and addressing emerging risks. 
 
The Board will continue to exercise prudent investment discipline and assess whether the 
Group has the necessary financial, operational and management capacity to undertake any 
proposed investment, with the objective of safeguarding shareholders' interests and supporting 
the Group's long-term development.

qa.question:
As noted in the chairman’s statement, Tong Guan Food Products Sdn. Bhd. recorded a 
1.6% decline in revenue to RM141.8 million, mainly due to lower sales of biscuits and 
cooking oil products. Swee Hin Chan Company Sdn. Berhad reported a 10.8% decline in 
revenue to RM82.6 million, primarily due to lower selling prices and sales volumes for starch 
products. The group also holds a 30% stake in United Malayan Flour (1996) Sdn. Bhd. (UMF), 
which is accounted for as an associate.  
 
Over the past five years, the group’s growth appears to have stagnated, with losses 
attributable to shareholders reported in the past four years and a shrinking shareholders’ 
equity base. 
 
(Source: company annual report; emphasis added) 
 
With the STI hitting new all-time highs in recent months, the company’s share price has 
steadily declined over the years and last traded at around $0.85 per share. According to SGX 
StockFacts, the price-to-book value ratio is approximately 0.4 times.  

(Source: https://investors.sgx.com/market/securities?code=K03&type=stocks&lang=en)

(i) 
Can the audit committee provide shareholders with greater clarity on the basis 
for determining the carrying value of $692,434 following the loss of significant 
influence, which resulted in a deemed disposal loss of $1,707,566 from the 
previous carrying amount of $2.4 million? What valuation methodology, 
assumptions and inputs were used, and was an independent valuation obtained? 
Company’s Response : 
The S$692,434 represented the Group’s equity-accounted carrying amount of 
its retained 19.96% interest in SGP at the date of reclassification, derived from 
the previous carrying amount after recognising SGP’s post-acquisition results 
and the effect of the relevant share issuances and dilution. 
At Company level, the investment had been carried at a cost of S$2.4 million. 
Its remeasurement to S$692,434 resulted in a Company-level deemed-disposal 
loss of S$1,707,566. 
At Group level, the carrying amount of S$902,420 as at 31 July 2025 was 
reduced by S$209,986, representing the Group’s share of SGP’s FY2026 losses, 
to S$692,434. As a cross-check, KGL’s 19.96% share of SGP’s NTA of 
S$3,579,672 based on SGP financial information dated 28 February 2026 was 
approximately S$714,503, about 3.2% above the carrying amount. 
No separate independent valuation was commissioned. The carrying amount 
was assessed by Management using SGP’s available financial information and 
the Group’s accounting records. 
(ii) 
At what valuation did the new investor subscribe for shares in SGP? Did the group 
have any pre-emptive or anti-dilution rights in relation to its SGP investment, and 
if so, on what basis did the board decide against making further investments into 
SGP? 
Company’s Response : 
The 99,404 shares issued to the new investor were subscribed for at 
approximately S$5.03 per share, for an aggregate consideration of 
approximately S$500,000, under SGP’s Series A funding arrangements. 
KGL held general pre-emptive rights under Clause 4 of SGP’s Shareholders’ 
Agreement. KGL and the relevant shareholders consented to or waived the 
applicable rights in connection with the relevant new investor and employee-
option issuances, subject to the terms of the Shareholders’ Agreement. No 
separate anti-dilution adjustment was applied to those issuances. 
KGL previously participated in SGP’s FY2025 fundraising by subscribing for 
179,013 shares for S$900,000, through cash payment and conversion of an 
existing shareholder loan. As disclosed in the FY2025 Annual Report, KGL’s 
interest declined in stages from 30.00% to 21.03% during FY2025. The further 
new-investor and employee-option issuances in FY2026 diluted KGL’s retained 
804,013 shares from approximately 21.03% to 19.96%. In deciding not to 
make an additional equity investment, the Board considered SGP’s performance 

6 
to date, its medium-term strategic plan and expected future funding 
requirements, KGL’s minority position and the Group’s capital priorities. 
iii) 
How was the current carrying value of $100,000, classified as a short-term 
unquoted equity investment (financial asset), determined, given the previous 
carrying value of $692,434 (as an associate)? What valuation methodology and 
assumptions were applied? 
Company’s Response : 
Upon the loss of significant influence over SGP, the Group ceased applying the 
equity method and reclassified its retained 19.96% interest as an unquoted 
equity investment measured at fair value through profit or loss under SFRS(I) 
9. The investment was classified as a short-term financial asset because the 
Board was pursuing its disposal and expected it to be realised within 12 
months. 
The S$100,000 carrying value as at 31 July 2026 was determined using a fair-
value approach. As disclosed in the FY2026 audited financial statements, the 
market-based assessment took into account SGP’s adjusted net tangible assets 
and KGL’s percentage shareholding. Management also considered SGP’s 
financial position, its funding requirements and the indicative market evidence 
available in assessing the value of KGL’s interest. The subsequent negotiated 
proposal for KGL’s entire shareholding was considered additional supporting 
evidence, to the extent that it reflected conditions existing as at 31 July 2026, 
although the agreement in principle was reached after that date. The 
S$100,000 consideration related to the shares; reimbursement of KGL’s 
shareholder loan and related interest was addressed separately. The resulting 
unrealised fair-value loss was S$592,434 against the previous carrying amount 
of S$692,434. 
As an additional downside consideration, the Board examined the potential 
effect of SGP’s proposed Rescue Financing Framework (the “Framework”). On 
the illustrative ownership basis of 19.86% used in that Framework, KGL’s 
interest could have fallen to approximately 0.3256% if it did not participate in 
further funding. At the Framework’s illustrative post-money valuation of 
S$610,000, that residual interest would have an indicative value of 
approximately S$1,986. This illustrated the potential further dilution and 
capital exposure if the Framework proceeded on its proposed terms without 
KGL’s participation. The figures were illustrative and did not represent a 
completed transaction or a separate valuation of KGL’s investment as at 31 July 
2026. The same material terms of the subsequent proposed disposal were 
offered to SGP’s eligible existing investor shareholders through the applicable 
right-of-first-refusal process, and no shareholder elected to acquire KGL’s 
shares. 

7 
On 28 August 2026, the company reached an agreement in principle with Mr Michael Chew, an 
executive director, in relation to the proposed disposal of its 804,013 shares in SGP. Under the 
proposed arrangement, Mr Michael Chew or another purchaser acceptable to the company would 
acquire the shares for a consideration of not less than $100,000. 
iv) 
Given the proposed transaction involves an executive director, how has the board 
assessed the fairness of the proposed consideration and managed the potential 
conflict of interest? What independent safeguards have been put in place to 
ensure that the disposal is conducted on an arm’s-length basis and in the 
interests of the company and its shareholders? 
Company’s Response : 
Mr Michael Chew disclosed his interest in the proposed disposal to the Board. 
He negotiated with KGL in his capacity as a prospective purchaser, but did not 
participate in the Independent Directors’ deliberations and decisions on behalf 
of KGL concerning the proposed disposal. 
The assessment was undertaken by the Independent Directors, who considered 
(1) SGP’s historical performance and expected future funding requirements, (2) 
the potential dilution and indicative residual value under the proposed 
Framework, (3) KGL’s financial exposure if it retained the investment, and (4) 
the terms available for an exit. They also considered the separate 
reimbursement of KGL’s S$148,927 shareholder loan and applicable interest, in 
addition to the S$100,000 consideration for KGL’s 804,013 shares. 
The Board did not rely solely on Mr Michael Chew’s offer. An earlier indicative 
expression of interest from an existing SGP shareholder was conditional upon 
KGL not participating in the proposed shareholder financing and did not provide 
definitive terms or transaction certainty. Mr Michael Chew subsequently made 
an offer to acquire KGL’s shareholding in SGP, and following further discussions 
and negotiations with the Independent Directors, the proposed consideration 
was increased to S$100,000. 
Pursuant to the right-of-first-refusal provisions in SGP’s Shareholders’ 
Agreement, KGL’s entire shareholding was offered to the eligible existing 
shareholders on the same material terms. No shareholder elected to acquire 
KGL’s shares. 
Having considered the above factors and the measures taken to manage Mr 
Michael Chew’s potential conflict of interest, the Independent Directors 
consider the proposed consideration commercially reasonable and the disposal 
to be in the interests of KGL and its shareholders, subject to the remaining 
applicable requirements

(ii) 
Given the company’s persistent losses and the board’s intention to reinvest capital, 
how does the board assess the merits of retaining and deploying further capital 
rather than returning capital to shareholders? What financial and strategic criteria 
must investments meet before capital is committed? Has the current management 
team demonstrated a track record of value creation through the group's operations 
and investments? 
Company’s Response : 
In considering whether to retain or return capital, the Board takes into account 
the Group’s working-capital and liquidity requirements, existing financial 
commitments, dividend-paying capacity and cash-flow outlook, alongside 
financial performance, capital requirements and strategic priorities. 
Before committing capital, the Board considers an investment’s strategic fit, 
funding requirements, expected returns and principal risks. It also considers 
whether continuing support is justified and may limit further funding, 
restructure or divest where the prospects no longer support additional 
exposure. 
The Board recognises TGF’s continued profitability and SHC’s return to 
profitability in FY2026. However, the Group’s operating results and investment 
performance have not consistently translated into satisfactory Group-level 
returns or shareholder value. Management’s performance will continue to be 
assessed against sustained profitability, cash generation, returns on capital and 
its willingness to restructure or exit low-return investments where commercially 
justified. 
(iii) 
Has the board undertaken a formal assessment of the company's optimal capital 
structure and the level of cash required to fund its operating needs? 
Company’s Response : 
The Company has not undertaken a separate formal study of its optimal capital 
structure or adopted a fixed cash-balance or gearing target. Nevertheless, the 
Board reviews the Group’s liquidity and capital requirements through annual 
budgeting, cash-flow forecasting and ongoing assessment of working capital, 
capital expenditure and funding commitments, taking account of trading 
volumes, inventories, receivables, market conditions and potential business 
opportunities. 
The Group’s trading and distribution businesses require liquidity to fund 
inventories, receivables and operating obligations, which fluctuate with market 
conditions. The Board will continue to assess the balance between financial 
flexibility, capital efficiency and shareholder returns.

automatically surplus cash available for distribution, having regard to liabilities,
